hints.title: Check both parts
hints.body: A counterexample must have an odd number of zeros between its two 1 s, and it must be composite.
hints.recap: Required form and failed primality are separate checks.
hints.pitfall: A composite number of the wrong form is irrelevant.
hints.pause: Count the interior zeros in each number.

hints.title: Separate the two tests
hints.body: For each displayed number, record the number of zeros and whether the stated factorisation makes the number composite.
hints.recap: A counterexample needs a true premise and a false conclusion.
hints.pitfall: A composite number with the wrong number of zeros does not test the claim.
hints.pause: Make a two-column table without selecting an option yet.

recall.reminder: A counterexample needs a true premise and a false conclusion.

hints.title: Use the counterexample criterion
hints.body: Inspect the rows in your table for numbers meeting the hypothesis but failing the conclusion.
hints.recap: Both parts of the counterexample criterion are required.
hints.pitfall: A prime example supports one instance; it does not disprove a universal claim.
hints.pause: Identify the qualifying rows and choose the matching option.

recall.reminder: Both parts of the counterexample criterion are required.

solution:
I: 101 has one zero, so it satisfies the premise, but it is prime and therefore does not contradict the conclusion.

II: 1001 is composite, but has two zeros. Its premise is false, so it is not a counterexample.

III: 10001 has three zeros and equals 73×137. It satisfies the required form but is not prime.

III only: D.
knowledgePattern: Check the antecedent digit pattern before using compositeness
